name: Rome
info: Rome is the capital and largest city of Italy, on the Tiber in Lazio. Traditionally founded in 753 BCE, it was capital of a kingdom, a republic and an empire, then seat of the popes.

facts.founded: Traditionally 21 April 753 BCE by Romulus, according to legend; archaeology shows villages joining into a city in the mid-8th century BCE
facts.where: On the Tiber in the Lazio region of central Italy, about 24 km inland from the Tyrrhenian Sea
facts.known: The founding legend of Romulus and Remus; capital of the Roman Republic and Empire; Augustus's rebuilding; the sacks of 410 and 455; seat of the popes and the Papal States; the Renaissance under Julius II; capital of Italy from 1871
facts.today: The capital and largest city of Italy, with Vatican City, an independent state, inside its boundaries.

t: According to tradition Rome was founded in 753 BCE, while the archaeology shows villages on its hills joining into a city in the mid-8th century BCE.
It was capital of a kingdom, a republic and an empire, and then lost people and standing through the Gothic Wars and the centuries of the Avignon Papacy.
The popes made it the centre of the Papal States and of the Renaissance, and it became the capital of the Kingdom of Italy in 1871.
dyk: Because Rome shrank so far in the Middle Ages, very significant ancient Roman remains survived in its centre, and Phocas's gift of the Pantheon to the Pope probably saved it from destruction.
ev: Traditional date of the founding by Romulus
Expulsion of the last king and start of the Republic, by tradition
Sack by the Senones under Brennus (390 in the traditional chronology)
Octavian is named Augustus, and the principate begins
Sack by the Visigoths under Alaric
Pepin gives the Pope the Duchy of Rome, creating the Papal States
Sack of Rome by the troops of Charles V
Italian troops enter through Porta Pia, and Rome becomes capital of Italy in 1871

sections.origins:
Rome stands in the Lazio region of central Italy on the Tiber, about 24 km inland from the Tyrrhenian Sea. The original settlement grew on hills facing a ford beside the Tiber Island, the only natural ford of the river in this area. The Rome of the Kings was later said to stand on seven hills: the Aventine, Caelian, Capitoline, Esquiline, Palatine, Quirinal and Viminal.

Archaeological evidence of human occupation of the area is about 14,000 years old, though a dense layer of later debris obscures the Palaeolithic and Neolithic sites. Between the end of the Bronze Age and the start of the Iron Age each hill held a village, and on the Capitoline one is attested from the end of the 14th century BCE. There is wide agreement that the city formed gradually by the joining of several villages around the largest, on the Palatine, and that this took place in the mid-8th century BCE. Trade with the Greek colonies of southern Italy, mainly Ischia and Cumae, helped the process. The view that Rome was founded deliberately in that century remains a fringe hypothesis.

Roman tradition told a different story. According to the annalists, the twins Romulus and Remus, suckled by a she-wolf, decided to build a city; after an argument Romulus killed his brother and the city took his name, on 21 April 753 BCE, the date later set by Varro. Virgil joined this legend to an older one in which the Trojan Aeneas escaped to Italy, and Strabo records further stories, that Evander led an Arcadian colony or that Greeks founded the city.
sections.growth:
Rome was large for a Latin settlement. Most of the bigger Early Iron Age cities of Latium covered 50 to 80 hectares, while Rome had reached about 200. By 550 BCE, according to one estimate, it covered about 285 hectares and held 35,000 people, though others put the population just under 100,000 between 600 and 500 BCE. It passed 300,000 by 150 BCE. The victory over Carthage in the First Punic War brought its first provinces outside the peninsula, and Rome became the capital of an overseas empire for the first time. In the 2nd century BCE farmers driven from their land by large slave-worked estates moved to the city in great numbers.

Under Augustus the city was rebuilt on a larger scale. He is said to have remarked that he found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble, and he added the Forum of Augustus and the Ara Pacis. The size of the city in his time is a matter of speculation. Glenn Storey estimates 450,000 people, Neville Morley roughly 800,000 and Whitney Oates 1.2 million, and estimates of its peak range from 450,000 to over 3.5 million, with 1 to 2 million most often favoured. The city was subsidised, with roughly 15 to 25 percent of its grain supply paid for by the state, and it depended on goods and taxes from the provinces. Commerce and industry mattered less than in Alexandria. In 98 CE, according to Frontinus, nine aqueducts fed 39 monumental fountains and 591 public basins. The population fell after the 2nd century, and when the Aurelian Wall was finished in 273 it was only around 500,000.
sections.rulers:
According to tradition seven kings ruled for 243 or 244 years: Romulus, Numa Pompilius, Tullus Hostilius, Ancus Marcius, Tarquinius Priscus, Servius Tullius and Tarquinius Superbus. The Gauls destroyed much of the city's records, and modern scholars treat the list as of doubtful value, though the last kings may be historical. The last three are said to have been Etruscan, and some historians believe Rome was under Etruscan influence for about a century. In 509 BCE, by tradition, the last king was expelled and an oligarchic republic led by two annual consuls was set up. Rome became the dominant city of Latium and then conquered the peninsula, and the Punic Wars (264 to 146 BCE) made it the leading power of the western Mediterranean.

Civil wars followed: Sulla, then Caesar, who crossed the Rubicon in January 49 BCE. After Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE, Octavian defeated Antony at Actium on 2 September 31 BCE, and in 27 BCE he was named Augustus. Diocletian's reforms deprived Rome of its role as administrative capital, and in 330 Constantine made Constantinople a second capital. The seat of the western government moved to Ravenna in 408, though from 450 the emperors mostly lived in Rome. Romulus Augustus was deposed on 4 September 476, and Rome passed to Odoacer, the Ostrogoths and, after the Gothic Wars, to the Eastern Roman Empire. From 756 the popes held the city as the centre of the Papal States, until Italian troops entered on 20 September 1870 and in 1871 Rome became the capital of Italy.
sections.life:
The city's early population was a mixture of Latins, Etruscans and Sabines. The Etruscans left a lasting mark: the Romans learned temple building from them, and the triad of Juno, Minerva and Jupiter may come from the Etruscan Uni, Menrva and Tinia, although Rome was primarily a Latin city and was also influenced by the Greek cities of the south. Religio Romana was the main religion of the city until Christianity, which reached Rome in the 1st century; Peter and Paul were martyred there, and the Bishops of Rome came to be seen by Catholics as successors of Peter. Rome also had mystery cults such as Mithraism. A Jewish community has lived in the city since the end of the Republic. It was based in Trastevere and then, by the order of Pope Paul IV, elected in 1555, confined to the Ghetto, where Jews wore yellow hats or veils and were locked in at night. The Ghetto was abolished in 1870.

From the 2nd century catacombs were cut in the soft tuff outside the city, because Roman law forbade burial within it. They hold Christian, pagan and Jewish burials. In the 7th century officials and churchmen from the eastern empire made the lay aristocracy and the Church leadership largely Greek speaking, and eleven of thirteen popes between 678 and 752 were of Greek or Syrian descent. In the Middle Ages great families such as the Annibaldi, Caetani, Colonna, Orsini and Conti fought each other from fortresses built over ancient buildings. Stones and marble were stripped from ancient buildings for lime and new churches, a practice that continued until the Renaissance.
sections.crises:
The Gauls under Brennus sacked Rome after the Battle of the Allia, in 387 BCE or, in the traditional chronology, 390. In 64 CE the Great Fire left much of the city destroyed, and Tacitus reports that Nero tried to put the blame on the Christians. The Antonine Plague is said to have killed 2,000 people a day. Alaric's Visigoths sacked the city on 24 August 410, Geiseric's Vandals on 2 June 455 and Ricimer's unpaid troops on 11 July 472. Jerome wrote that "The City which had taken the whole world was itself taken." The damage may have been overestimated, but from 439 the loss of grain from North Africa shrank the city. Estimates give 800,000 around 400, 500,000 by 452 and 80,000 to 100,000 around 500, though the figure may be twice that.

Rome changed hands several times in the Gothic Wars. It withstood a year-long siege in 537 and 538, and Totila sacked it on 17 December 546. Narses took it for good in 552. The drainage systems failed, low districts turned into marsh, malaria developed, and the population may have fallen to 30,000. A flood in 589 and a plague in 590 followed. Rome was sacked by the Normans in 1084, and in 1527 imperial troops of Charles V killed some 1,000 defenders and pillaged the city for days; only 42 of 189 Swiss Guards survived. During the Avignon Papacy from 1309 to 1377 the city decayed and held under 20,000 people. The bombing of San Lorenzo on 19 July 1943 caused about 3,000 deaths. The Germans declared Rome an open city on 14 August 1943 and it was liberated on 4 June 1944.
sections.legacy:
Rome is called one of the cradles of Western civilisation and Western Christian culture. Roman law influenced many modern legal systems, Latin gave rise to the Romance languages, and the Roman alphabet is the writing system used by the most languages. The poet Tibullus is reported to have first called the city the Eternal City, and Caput Mundi, capital of the world, was also used. Because the city shrank so far in the Middle Ages, very significant ancient remains survived in its centre, some abandoned and some still in use, among them the Colosseum, the Roman Forum and the Pantheon, which Phocas gave to the Pope and which probably escaped destruction as a result.

Later periods added their own layers. The popes made Rome the centre of the Renaissance in the later 15th century and under Julius II, Leo X and Clement VII; Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling, and a new St Peter's replaced Constantine's basilica. Sixtus V and the Baroque popes cut new streets and built fountains such as the Trevi, begun in 1732. The Lateran Treaty of 1929 created Vatican City, an independent state within the city. Today Rome is the capital and largest city of Italy, with about 2.7 million people in the municipality, and the seat of the Italian government and parliament.

summary: Rome grew from villages on the Tiber hills, traditionally founded in 753 BCE, into the capital of a republic and an empire. It shrank through sacks and wars to a small town among ruins, became the seat of the popes and a centre of the Renaissance, and in 1871 the capital of Italy.
references: Christopher Hibbert, Rome: the biography of a city (Penguin, 1987)
Gary Forsythe, A critical history of early Rome: from prehistory to the first Punic War (University of California Press, 2005)
Mary Beard, SPQR: A History of Ancient Rome (Liveright Publishing, 2015)
J. B. Bury, History of the Later Roman Empire: From the Death of Theodosius I (BiblioLife, 2009)
notes: Founding date: both articles give 21 April 753 BCE as the annalists' date and the mid-8th century BCE as the archaeological birth; start is -753 with circa true.
Sack by the Gauls: the history article gives 390 BCE for the Battle of the Allia (Polybius 387/386) and elsewhere 387 BCE; I wrote 387 BCE or, in the traditional chronology, 390.
Length of the monarchy: city article 244 years, history article 243 (Varro); I wrote 243 or 244.

Population around 400: the city article gives 800,000 (Krautheimer) and the history article says no fewer than 650,000 in the mid-5th century (Jones); I gave 800,000 around 400, 500,000 by 452 and 80,000 to 100,000 around 500 as hedged estimates. Gothic Wars low: 30,000 (history) against 35,000 (city); I used 30,000 with 'may have'.
Gothic Wars: history article says the Ostrogoths retook Rome in 549, city article says 546 and 550; I gave only 546 and 552.
Roman Republic of 1798 to 1799 (history) against 1798 to 1800 (city); left out.
Great Fire of 64: city article says two-thirds ruined, history article 'much of the city destroyed'; I used the latter.
Sack of 410: city article says very little physical damage, history article that damage may have been overestimated; I wrote 'may have been overestimated'.

Left out: Trajan's expansion, the Normans' sack detail, Fascism, the Lateran Treaty details beyond one sentence, the Sutri donation of 729, and the present-day economy, transport and sport. 'Eternal City' is given only as a name Tibullus is reported to have first used.
